# The Night Attendant

The laundromat on Carver Street never closes, which means someone has to be there when it isn't open to anyone in particular. For eleven months that someone has been me.

The job is mostly watching. I refill the soap dispenser, which hasn't worked since before I was hired, so really I just open it and look inside. I sweep lint from under the dryers. Lint is the most honest substance in the world: it's just what falls off of people when they spin. Cotton, hair, the fuzz of a sweater someone's grandmother knitted, the pale blue of hospital scrubs. I sweep it all into the same bin.

Between two and five in the morning, the customers are a particular kind of person. The drunk college kids come earlier, around midnight, laughing and dropping quarters. By two it's the ones who can't sleep or can't go home. A nurse coming off a double. A cab driver who washes the same three shirts every few days and reads paperbacks with the covers torn off. A woman who brings everything she owns in two garbage bags and sits very straight while it dries, as if posture were a kind of address.

And on Tuesdays, at three, the man with the small shirt.

He started coming in March. Mid-forties, work boots, a jacket too thin for the season. He'd walk in carrying nothing but a plastic grocery bag, and from it he'd take a single child's T-shirt. Yellow, with a cartoon dinosaur on the front, the kind with big eyes that make even a tyrannosaur look apologetic. He'd put it in machine number seven, always seven, feed in four quarters, and sit down to watch it turn.

One shirt, in a machine built for twenty pounds of laundry. It looked absurd in there, a tiny yellow flag tumbling alone through all that water.

I didn't ask. That's the first rule of the night shift, one nobody tells you but everyone learns: at three in the morning, people are carrying things you can't see, and asking about them is like grabbing someone's arm on a staircase. You might think you're helping. You might make them fall.

So I made up stories instead. The boy was in the hospital, and the man washed the shirt so it would be clean when he came home. The boy lived with his mother now, in another state, and the shirt was the one thing left behind. The boy was fine, asleep at home, and the man just liked the machine's rhythm, the way some people like trains. I preferred that last story. I told it to myself most often, which is how I knew it wasn't true.

Here is what I noticed over the weeks. He never used the dryer. When the wash finished, he'd take the shirt out, wet, fold it into a square on the folding table, smoothing it with the flat of his hand, and put it back in the grocery bag. Then he'd leave. The whole thing took thirty-four minutes. I timed it once and felt ashamed afterward, like I'd read someone's mail.

In August, the dinosaur started to fade. A shirt can only go through so much. The yellow got paler, the seams went soft, and one Tuesday I saw a small hole near the collar where the fabric had simply given up. He saw it too. He stood at the folding table for a long time with his thumb over the hole, as if he could keep it from being there.

That was the night I broke the rule.

I didn't say anything wise. I don't have anything wise. I said, "Seven's the gentlest machine, if that helps. The others agitate too hard."

It was true. I'd learned the machines the way you learn the moods of the people you live with. Number three shakes. Number twelve eats socks. Seven is slow and steady, older than the others, with a sound like someone humming under their breath.

He looked at me, and for a second I thought I'd done it, grabbed the arm and made him fall. Then he nodded.

"I know," he said. "That's why."

That was all. He folded the shirt and went out into the dark.

The next Tuesday, he didn't come. Nor the one after. I told myself the good story, the boy is fine, the boy came home, the shirt doesn't need washing anymore because someone is wearing it, and I told it so many times it wore thin in my hands like fabric.

In October he came back. Three o'clock, same jacket, a heavier grocery bag. He nodded to me as he passed. At machine seven he took out a small pair of jeans, two shirts, one with a rocket and one plain green, some socks balled together, and a pair of pajamas printed with moons. He fed in the quarters and sat down.

When the wash finished, he moved it all to the dryer.

I watched the clothes turn behind the round glass window, a small, crowded galaxy. I don't know what happened in those weeks. I don't know if the boy came home, or if there was a different boy, or if the man had finally just decided to do the laundry of someone who was still here. The rule holds. I didn't ask.

But when the dryer stopped, he pulled everything out warm, and I saw him press the moon pajamas to his face for just a moment, the way you do when something smells like it's been taken care of.

Then he folded everything, stacked it neatly in the bag, and left.

I swept under the dryers after. There was lint in the trap: a little gray, a little green, and a few threads of faded yellow that must have been caught in the machine since summer. I held them for a while before I threw them away.

Everything falls off of us when we spin. The trick, I think, is that something stays.
